summary: Odd-parity encoded logical gates in coupled fluxonium qubits benefit from spatially correlated longitudinal TLS noise, which converts harmful differential fluctuations into common-mode components. Projecting the two-qubit Hamiltonian onto the subspace $\{|01\rangle, |10\rangle\}$ yields logical $X_L$ and $Z_L$ rotations driven by exchange coupling and detuning, with encoded gate fidelity monotonically improving as noise correlation coefficient $\rho$ increases.
motivation: Fluxonium platforms exhibit millisecond coherence and large anharmonicity ($|\alpha|/2\pi \sim 5$ GHz) but host non-Markovian TLS defects in Josephson junctions. The question is whether correlated TLS environments can be exploited rather than passively endured for encoded logical control.
method: The authors project the exchange-coupled two-fluxonium Hamiltonian with capacitive coupling onto the odd-parity subspace, decomposing correlated Gaussian Ornstein-Uhlenbeck TLS noise with memory time $\tau_c$ into common-mode and differential components. They benchmark encoded $X_L(\pi)$ and $Z_L(\pi)$ gates via average gate fidelity $F_\mathrm{avg}$ under Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, Markovian, and random-telegraph noise models, and supplement with logical dynamical decoupling.
result: For symmetric noise ($\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = 0.30$ MHz$/(2\pi)$) and $\tau_c = 1$ µs, encoded gate fidelity increases monotonically with $\rho$; the gate infidelity 1−$F_\mathrm{avg}$ decreases approximately exponentially in the strongly correlated regime. This improvement persists across all three noise models and remains visible under exchange/detuning control errors ($\epsilon_J, \epsilon_\Delta$), with additional gains from logical CPMG-4 and XY4 refocusing at intermediate correlations.
